data.title: Melasma — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 16 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Melasma** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. Define melasma.**
- Acquired, chronic, relapsing, symmetrical hypermelanosis of sun-exposed skin (mostly face) with light- to dark-brown irregular macules and patches; common in women of reproductive age with Fitzpatrick types III–V (Indian, Hispanic, Asian)

**Q2. Aetiological factors.**
- UV and visible light (high-energy visible/blue light — esp. in darker skin), heat
- Hormonal: pregnancy (chloasma/'mask of pregnancy'), oral contraceptives, hormone replacement, thyroid autoimmunity
- Genetic: family history in ~50%
- Others: cosmetics (perfumes — photosensitising), phototoxic drugs (anticonvulsants), stress, ovarian disorders

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Not merely melanocyte hyperactivity: photo-aged dermis (solar elastosis), increased vascularity (VEGF, endothelin-1), mast cells, disrupted basement membrane (pendulous melanocytes, dermal melanin drop), increased α-MSH, SCF/c-KIT, Wnt signalling, sebocyte factors — 'photoageing disorder of susceptible skin'

**Q4. Clinical patterns.**
- Centrofacial (forehead, cheeks, nose, upper lip, chin — commonest, ~60%), malar (cheeks and nose), mandibular (jawline), extrafacial (forearms, V of neck — older women)
- By depth (old Wood's lamp classification): epidermal (enhanced contrast — better prognosis), dermal (no enhancement — poor), mixed (commonest); now replaced by dermoscopy/RCM

**Q5. Discuss causes of facial hyperpigmentation (PYQ).**
- Melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (acne), Riehl's melanosis (pigmented contact dermatitis — cosmetics, kumkum), lichen planus pigmentosus, ashy dermatosis, nevus of Ota/Hori's naevus (acquired bilateral naevus of Ota-like macules), freckles/lentigines, drug-induced (minocycline, amiodarone, antimalarials, phenytoin, chlorpromazine, clofazimine), exogenous ochronosis (hydroquinone misuse), acanthosis nigricans (face), periorbital hyperpigmentation, frictional melanosis, phytophotodermatitis, Addison's disease, haemochromatosis, erythromelanosis follicularis faciei, maturational dyschromia, topical steroid-induced dyspigmentation

**Q6. How do you assess severity?**
- MASI (Melasma Area and Severity Index — area, darkness, homogeneity in forehead 30%, right malar 30%, left malar 30%, chin 10%; 0–48), modified MASI (area + darkness; 0–24), MELASQOL (quality of life)
- Dermoscopy: brown pseudo-network (epidermal), blue-grey granules (dermal), telangiectasia, sparing of follicles

**Q7. Histopathology.**
- Increased epidermal melanin (basal and suprabasal), enlarged dendritic melanocytes (not necessarily increased number), dermal melanophages, solar elastosis, increased vessels and mast cells, basement membrane damage

**Q8. Discuss treatment of melasma (PYQ: depigmenting agents — indications, side effects).**
- Strict photoprotection: broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF ≥30 with UVA protection and tinted (iron oxide) for visible light, reapplied every 2–3 h; physical protection; stop OCP/ photosensitising cosmetics
- First-line topical: triple combination cream (Kligman's modified — hydroquinone 4% + tretinoin 0.05% + fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%) nightly for up to 8–12 weeks then maintenance with non-steroid agents (avoid prolonged unsupervised use — steroid damage, ochronosis)
- Hydroquinone 2–4% (tyrosinase inhibitor; side effects — irritation, contact dermatitis, exogenous ochronosis with long-term high strength, confetti depigmentation)
- Non-hydroquinone agents: azelaic acid 15–20%, kojic acid, arbutin, tranexamic acid (topical), cysteamine 5%, niacinamide 4%, thiamidol, licorice extract, vitamin C, retinoids, methimazole, glutathione (topical)
- Oral tranexamic acid 250 mg twice daily for 3–6 months (plasmin inhibitor — reduces melanocyte stimulation and vascularity; check for thromboembolic risk, avoid in pregnancy/OCP use/clotting disorders); Polypodium leucotomos
- Procedures (adjuncts, cautious in dark skin): chemical peels — glycolic acid 20–70%, salicylic 20–30%, lactic, Jessner's, TCA low strength; microneedling with tranexamic acid; lasers — low-fluence Q-switched Nd:YAG (laser toning), picosecond, fractional non-ablative, PDL for vascular component; risk of rebound and mottled hypopigmentation

**Q9. What is exogenous ochronosis?**
- Blue-black/slate-grey speckled pigmentation with 'caviar-like' papules on sites of long-term hydroquinone (or phenol, resorcinol, antimalarial) use — inhibits homogentisic acid oxidase locally; histology — yellow-brown banana-shaped fibres in dermis; very difficult to treat (stop agent, sunscreens, Q-switched lasers, CO2)

**Q10. Prognosis.**
- Chronic and relapsing (especially with sun exposure); pregnancy melasma may fade after delivery; dermal component resistant; maintenance therapy and sun protection lifelong

**Q11. Describe dermoscopic patterns of melasma and their use.**
- Light brown homogeneous pseudo-network (epidermal), dark-brown dots/ globules, blue-grey granules (dermal), telangiectatic vessels (vascular component — consider tranexamic acid/ PDL), sparing of follicles; guides therapy and prognosis — better than Wood's lamp

**Q12. Chemical peels for melasma — which and how?**
- Glycolic acid 20–70% (start low, 2–4 weekly), salicylic acid 20–30%, lactic acid, mandelic acid, Jessner's, modified Jessner's, TCA 10–15%, yellow (retinoic acid) peel; series of 4–6 peels with home triple combination and sunscreen; risk of PIH and irritation in dark skin — prime with hydroquinone 2 weeks before

**Q13. Laser toning — what is it and risks?**
- Low-fluence Q-switched Nd:YAG 1064 nm (large spot, multiple passes, weekly) — sub-cellular selective photothermolysis of melanosomes; risks: mottled hypopigmentation (confetti), rebound hyperpigmentation, relapse; combine with topicals, not first line

**Q14. What is the role of glutathione (oral/IV) for melasma?**
- Antioxidant that shifts eumelanin to pheomelanin; oral/ topical glutathione has modest evidence; IV glutathione for skin lightening is not approved (FDA/ CDSCO warnings) — risks of liver/ kidney toxicity, SJS, anaphylaxis; should not be advised

**Q15. Melasma in men — features.**
- ~10% of cases; similar patterns (malar commonest), sun exposure and family history main factors; lower hormonal association; treat similarly

**Q16. What are the quality-of-life tools and counselling points?**
- MELASQOL (10-item, 7-point scale); counsel chronicity, maintenance with sunscreen (including visible light), realistic expectations, avoid unsupervised steroid-containing creams (topical steroid damaged face), and avoid OTC hydroquinone misuse

## Quick spotter facts
- Symmetrical brown facial patches in a woman, worse with sun/pregnancy — melasma
- Triple combination + sunscreen first line; oral tranexamic acid
- Long hydroquinone misuse → exogenous ochronosis

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Melasma); Indian/Pigmentary Disorders Society consensus on melasma. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
